title: Units, international units and millimoles on labels and prescriptions
blurb: Work with doses in units and millimoles from the strength on the label, write "units" safely and enter the answer in the right box.
question: A bag of 0.9% sodium chloride 1000 mL contains potassium chloride 40 mmol and runs at 125 mL per hour. How many millimoles of potassium does the person receive each hour?

teach.h: Units and millimoles are amounts too
teach.body: Some medicines are measured by biological activity in units (insulin, heparin, oxytocin, nystatin) rather than by mass. Electrolytes such as potassium are measured in millimoles (mmol), an amount of substance. Plain English: treat "units" and "mmol" exactly like mg. The label tells you how many are in each mL, and the same want over have arithmetic applies. You cannot convert units to mg unless the label gives an equivalence.

head: Medicine
Label strength

teach.caption: Strengths are always given on the label or in the question: never work from memory.

steps.label: Want ÷ have
steps.sub: same units on top and bottom

items: Staff nurse Priya Sharma checks a bag: potassium chloride 40 mmol in 1000 mL, running at 125 mL per hour.
Concentration: 40 mmol ÷ 1000 mL = 0.04 mmol in each mL.
Check another way: 1000 mL at 125 mL per hour lasts 8 hours; 40 ÷ 8 = 5 mmol per hour.
She enters 5 in the number-only box with "mmol" printed after it.

teach.body: Write "units" in full. A handwritten "U" can be read as a 0, so 10U becomes 100: a tenfold overdose. "IU" can be misread as IV or 10. Labels sometimes print IU (the midwifery practice paper shows "40 IU of Syntocinon"), so recognise it, but record the dose as units. On Part A, answers in units and mmol go in number-only boxes: digits only, no commas.

teach.text: "U" misread as "0" turns 6U into 60: a tenfold error. Also, a label of 5,000 units/mL is typed in a number box as 5000: the comma makes the box reject the entry.

items: Units and mmol use the same arithmetic as mg.
The label strength is your "have"; it is always given.
Write "units" in full; U and IU are misread.
Rate x concentration gives the amount per hour.
Number-only boxes: digits and a point, no commas, no unit.

summary: You can now read strengths in units and millimoles from a label, calculate an amount or a volume with the same method you use for milligrams, and record units safely without abbreviations.

A.q: A heparin label reads 1,000 units/mL. How many units are in 0.6 mL?
A.why: 1000 units per mL x 0.6 mL = 600 units.

whyNot.1: Tenfold error the other way: 1000 x 0.6 is 600.
whyNot.3: Added 0.6 mL as if it were 600 units to the 1000.

A.q: A bag is labelled potassium chloride 20 mmol in 500 mL. How many millimoles are in 125 mL?
A.why: 125 mL is a quarter of 500 mL, so 20 ÷ 4 = 5 mmol. Or 125 ÷ 500 x 20 = 5 mmol.

whyNot.0: This is the amount in 250 mL, not 125 mL.
whyNot.3: This is the amount in 62.5 mL; 125 mL is a quarter of the bag.

A.q: Your answer is twenty-five thousand units. The number-only box has "units" printed after it. What do you type?

whyNot.0: Commas are rejected by number-only boxes.
whyNot.1: The unit is already printed; the box takes digits only.
whyNot.2: Spaces are not accepted in a number-only box.

B.q: An adult is prescribed 18 units of insulin. The insulin is labelled 100 units/mL. What volume contains the dose? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
B.why: 18 units ÷ 100 units x 1 mL = 0.18 mL. Insulin is given with an insulin syringe or pen marked in units.

B.q: A woman's infusion contains oxytocin 40 units in 500 mL and runs at 125 mL per hour. How many units does she receive each hour?
B.why: 40 ÷ 500 = 0.08 units per mL. 0.08 x 125 = 10 units per hour.

whyNot.0: This is the amount in 1 mL, not in 125 mL.
whyNot.2: Divided 500 by 40; units per hour = units per mL x mL per hour.

B.q: An adult is prescribed enoxaparin 4000 units. The syringe is labelled 100 mg/mL, and the label states 1 mg is equivalent to 100 units. What volume is needed? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
B.why: 4000 units ÷ 100 = 40 mg. 40 mg ÷ 100 mg x 1 mL = 0.4 mL.

whyNot.1: Tenfold error the other way: 40 ÷ 100 is 0.4.
whyNot.2: Gave the dose in mg (40) as the volume.

C.q: A 1000 mL bag contains potassium chloride 40 mmol and runs at 125 mL per hour. How many millimoles of potassium does the person receive each hour?
C.why: 40 ÷ 1000 = 0.04 mmol per mL. 0.04 x 125 = 5 mmol per hour.

whyNot.1: Divided 125 by 40; multiply the concentration by the rate.
whyNot.2: This is the run time in hours (1000 ÷ 125), not mmol.
whyNot.3: Divided 1000 by 40; that is mL per mmol.

C.q: A woman is prescribed nystatin oral suspension 1 mL four times a day for 7 days. The label reads 100,000 units/mL. How many units will she receive over the full course?
C.why: Per day: 100000 x 4 = 400000 units. Course: 400000 x 7 = 2800000 units.

whyNot.0: This is one day's total; the course is 7 days.
whyNot.1: Dropped a zero: 100000 x 4 x 7 is 2800000.
whyNot.3: Counted one dose a day; she takes four.

C.q: An adult has a heparin infusion of 25,000 units in 50 mL running at 2 mL per hour. How many units per hour is the person receiving?
C.why: 25000 ÷ 50 = 500 units per mL. 500 x 2 = 1000 units per hour.

whyNot.0: This is the amount in 1 mL; the rate is 2 mL per hour.
whyNot.1: Divided 25000 by 2; multiply the concentration by the rate.
whyNot.3: Multiplied 25000 by 2 without dividing by the 50 mL.

reteach.title: Pretend it says mg
reteach.question: If the label said 40 mg in 1000 mL, how would you find the amount in 125 mL?

blocks.h: Swap the word, keep the method
blocks.body: Cover the word "units" or "mmol" and read it as mg. The method you already know works unchanged: amount = concentration x volume, and volume = want ÷ have x stock volume. Then put the original unit back on the answer.

blocks.text: Write the word "units" every time; never let it shrink to U.

explain.body: U can look like 0 and IU like IV or 10. Record doses as "units".

test.q: Which record of a 10 unit insulin dose is safest?
test.why: Writing "units" in full removes the risk of a tenfold misreading.

whyNot.1: U can be read as 0, giving 100.
whyNot.2: IU can be misread as IV or as 10.
whyNot.3: A lower-case u can also be read as 0.

explain.body: Amount = strength per mL x volume. 100 units/mL x 0.25 mL = 25 units.

test.q: Insulin is labelled 100 units/mL. How many units are in 0.25 mL?

whyNot.1: Tenfold error the other way: 100 x 0.25 is 25.
whyNot.2: Divided 100 by 0.25; multiply strength by volume.

explain.h: Volume for a number of mmol
explain.body: Volume = mmol wanted ÷ mmol in stock x stock volume.

test.q: A 10 mL ampoule contains 20 mmol. What volume contains 15 mmol? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.2: Divided 15 by 20 and forgot to multiply by 10 mL.
whyNot.3: Inverted the fraction and forgot to multiply by 10 mL.

explain.text: A U read as a 0 multiplies the dose by ten.

test.q: A handwritten insulin dose "6U" is misread as 60 units. How many times the intended dose is that? Write your answer as a whole number.

whyNot.1: This is the intended dose, not the factor.
whyNot.2: 60 is ten times 6, not a hundred times.
whyNot.3: This is the difference in units, not the factor.
